questions.text: When several people need help, understanding each person's hardship makes me care about their situation.
I detect when a person uses physical touch, like a pat on the back, to establish a hierarchy rather than express warmth.
I tend to be the first person in a room to react emotionally to what's happening.
I tend to measure my week by how much I advanced my own objectives.
When I consider people with competing needs, I care about the suffering each person is experiencing.
I blend research, creation, and revision together fluidly rather than working in distinct phases.
I trust that the group will eventually resolve its own circular discussions.
I tend to emerge from stressful periods without the accumulated tension that others describe.
I handle commitments as they surface throughout the week without a formal review.
I tend not to notice when two people share a meaningful look during a conversation.
I tend to be unaware of the subtle ways people express loyalty to each other in group settings.
I tend to put others' comfort ahead of efficiency when the two conflict.
I consider multiple possible outcomes before committing to a decision.
I tend to unilaterally escalate issues when I think a group is underreacting.
I find myself noticing the cadence and rhythm of a conversation, not just the words.
I can tell when someone is smiling with their mouth but not with the muscles around their eyes.
I feel most proud of the things I did for others, not the things I achieved for myself.
I routinely opt for premium personal experiences—travel, dining, learning—because I believe I am worth it.
I build transition rituals between activities to stay grounded and focused.
I feel little concern for suffering in places I have never been.
I experience the end of a vacation or a visit with someone I love as a sharp, almost physical loss.
Someone's suffering usually has to be severe before it matters to me.
My internal state has a steadiness that I've come to recognize as simply the way I'm built.
I often adapt to the norms and expectations already present in a group.
I typically introduce structure to group work before anyone else does.
Even after hearing exactly what a person has endured, I feel little concern about what happens to them.
I prefer to move fast and fix errors when they surface rather than reviewing obsessively.
I am the one who typically opens a meeting by framing the key question.
I tend to seek out roles and projects that will look good on my own record.
I think of my future self as someone I am actively building conditions for.
I do not naturally detect when someone uses a group's shared values or language to gain credibility.
I experience reunion with people I care about as warm and welcome without it being an emotional avalanche.
I notice that the anticipation of seeing someone I've missed builds to a physical crescendo in my chest.
When someone is hurting, I want their pain to end.
I find that the thought of others benefiting from my effort is the strongest motivation I know.
I enjoy knowing that a project can succeed regardless of whether I am personally driving it.
